query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In rare‐earth‐free high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) for magnetic refrigeration, a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields is governed by a refined nanostructure where a fine grain size combined with uniformly distributed nano-precipitates (serving as local magnetoelastic sites) reduces local energy barriers for spin reorientation and facilitates a nearly second-order magnetic phase transition. This microstructure not only promotes a high magnetic entropy change at low fields but also supports rapid heat exchange, low magnetic hysteresis, and mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified or rapidly solidified high-entropy alloy with fine grain structure and nanoscale precipitates similar to those observed in SLM-built CoCrFeMnNi alloys.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-synthesis heat treatment to incrementally coarsen or partially dissolve the nano-precipitates, thereby altering the grain boundary density and precipitate size distribution.
generation.conditions: Tests performed near the magnetic transition temperature (e.g., room temperature ± 20°C) under low applied magnetic fields (e.g., <1 T), while monitoring both magnetic and thermal properties as well as mechanical behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The size and uniformity of nano-precipitates and fine grain boundaries that mediate local magnetoelastic strain fields.
generation.mechanism: The nano-precipitates act as nucleation sites for localized changes in magnetic order by inducing local strain fields that lower the energy barrier for domain reorientation. This facilitates a strong, reversible magnetocaloric effect with minimal hysteresis. Moreover, the fine grain structure promotes efficient thermal conduction and maintains mechanical integrity under cyclic loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (alloys with coarser precipitates and larger grains obtained via extended annealing), alloys retaining the refined nanostructure (fine grains with uniformly distributed nano-precipitates) will exhibit a significantly higher magnetic entropy change (ΔSM) at low applied fields, reduced magnetic hysteresis, and preserved mechanical stability with rapid heat exchange.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples subjected to prolonged annealing that leads to coarsened precipitates and larger grains.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for rare-earth-free HEAs operating near their magnetic transition conditions (typically around room temperature) under relatively low magnetic fields (<1 T) and within compositional ranges similar to those used in the experimental system.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between precipitate size distribution and the magnitude of the magnetocaloric effect is not fully established and may vary with alloy composition. Further experimental calibration is needed to determine the optimal nanostructural characteristics for maximal performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical rare-earth-free HEA samples and subject them to varied post-synthesis heat treatments designed to systematically increase precipitate size while affecting grain size. Characterize their microstructures using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Measure their magnetocaloric properties (e.g., magnetic entropy change ΔSM) and hysteresis loops under low applied magnetic fields (<1 T) near the transition temperature. Also, assess thermal conductivity and mechanical stability.
measurements: Nano-precipitate size distribution and grain size (via TEM/SEM)
Magnetic entropy change (ΔSM) versus applied magnetic field
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the precipitate size (or coarsening the nanostructure) does not lead to a measurable decrease in the magnetocaloric response (i.e., ΔSM remains equally high) and does not lead to an increase in magnetic hysteresis or degradation in thermal/mechanical properties compared to the baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism linking nanostructural refinement with enhanced magnetocaloric performance is falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
